a

Words: 134 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 134
a OurBigBook.com
A splitting field of f over F is an extension field in which f factors into linear factors and which is generated over F by those roots. The generation requirement excludes unnecessary extra elements.
For existence, induct on the degree. An irreducible factor p of f gives a field F1​=F[X]/(p), since an irreducible polynomial generates a maximal ideal in the polynomial ring over a field. The class α of X is a root of p and hence of f. By the factor theorem, f=(X−α)g over F1​, with degg=degf−1. Induction gives a splitting field of g over F1​. It contains all roots of f; taking the subfield generated by these roots over F gives exactly a splitting field of f. The degree-one case is immediate. Thus
Every positive-degree polynomial over a field has a splitting field.​
(1)

b

Words: 121 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 121
b OurBigBook.com
Over F2​, the cubic takes value one at both zero and one, so it has no root. A reducible cubic over a field has a linear factor and therefore a root; hence this cubic is irreducible. Adjoin a root:
K=F2​[α],α3+α+1=0.
(2)
This extension has basis 1,α,α2, degree three and eight elements. Squaring preserves polynomial equations with coefficients in F2​, so α2 and α4 are roots too. The nonzero element α is not one; the multiplicative group has prime order seven, so α has order seven. The exponents 1,2,4 are distinct modulo seven, making these three roots distinct. Thus they are all the roots and already lie in K. Therefore
The splitting field is F8​=F2​[X]/(X3+X+1),[K:F2​]=3.​
(3)

A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 92
c OurBigBook.com
All roots are ±2​ and ±3​, so the splitting field is K=Q(2​,3​). We have [Q(2​):Q]=2.
To show that adjoining 3​ doubles the degree, suppose 3​=a+b2​ with rational a,b. Squaring and using irrationality of 2​ gives ab=0. If b=0, then a2=3; if a=0, then b2=3/2. Neither is a rational square, as the prime exponents in a rational square are even. Thus 3​∈/Q(2​). Its quadratic polynomial remains irreducible over that field, and the tower law gives
K=Q(2​,3​),[K:Q]=4.​
(4)
A basis is 1,2​,3​,6​.

a OurBigBook.com
A composition series is a finite chain 1=G0​⊲G1​⊲⋯⊲Gr​=G in which each inclusion is proper, each subgroup is normal in the next, and every quotient Gi​/Gi−1​ is a nontrivial simple group. These quotients are the composition factors.
For a finite group, use induction on its order. The trivial group has the empty series. Otherwise choose a maximal proper normal subgroup N; such a subgroup exists because there are finitely many subgroups and 1 is proper. The correspondence theorem says normal subgroups of G/N correspond to normal subgroups of G containing N, so maximality makes G/N simple. Inductively construct a composition series of the smaller group N and append G. This proves existence.
A nonabelian example with abelian factors is
1⊲A3​⊲S3​,factors C3​,C2​.​
(5)
Both factors are simple because their orders are prime.

b

Words: 74 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 74
b OurBigBook.com
The cyclic group of order six has two different composition series:
1⊲C2​⊲C6​,1⊲C3​⊲C6​.​
(6)
Their factor lists are C2​,C3​ and C3​,C2​ respectively; normality follows from commutativity.
The Jordan–Hölder theorem states that any two composition series of a group have the same length and the same multiset of composition factors up to isomorphism. Equivalently, the factors of one series can be reordered to match those of the other by group isomorphisms. The actual intermediate subgroups need not be the same.

c

Words: 71 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 71
c OurBigBook.com
Let Cn​=⟨g⟩ and take H=⟨gp⟩. Since n=mp, the order of gp is m, so H≅Cm​. All subgroups of a cyclic group are normal. The quotient is generated by gH and has order n/m=p, giving
Cn​/H≅Cp​.​
(7)
A group of prime order has no nontrivial proper subgroup. By the subgroup correspondence theorem, no normal subgroup lies strictly between H and Cn​. Thus H is a maximal proper normal subgroup.

d

Words: 110 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 110
d OurBigBook.com
Given a prime factorization n=p1​⋯pr​, repeatedly apply part (c) to the cyclic group of order n: it has a chain of subgroups of successive orders
n,n/p1​,n/(p1​p2​),…,1.
(8)
Read in increasing order, this is a composition series with factors isomorphic to the cyclic groups of orders p1​,…,pr​. Any second prime factorization of the same integer produces another composition series of the same group Cn​.
The Jordan–Hölder theorem equates the two multisets of simple factors. Since Cp​≅Cq​ for primes p,q implies p=q by equality of group orders, the two prime multisets agree. Hence
The prime factorization is unique up to permutation.​
(9)
For n=1 both factor lists are empty, corresponding to the trivial group.

(cb​)=(bc​)(−1)∑i,j​[(pi​−1)/2][(qj​−1)/2].

k≡1(mod4),k≡1(modb),k≡c(modq).

iii OurBigBook.com
An integer square is a square modulo every prime, with the zero class allowed at primes dividing the integer. Conversely, suppose an odd integer a is not an integer square. If every prime exponent in ∣a∣ is even, the nonsquare condition forces a=−b2, handled by part (i). Otherwise some odd prime has an odd exponent, so a=±qtb as in part (ii). In either case there is a positive odd k with (a/k)=−1.
Factor k into odd primes. A product of Legendre symbols equalling minus one has at least one factor equal to minus one. Thus a fails to be a square modulo one of those primes, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence
a∈Z odd is an integer square iff x2≡a(modp) is solvable for every prime p.​
(24)
The solvability formulation makes explicit the zero-residue convention needed by the printed final assertion. The prime two causes no extra issue because every odd integer is one modulo two.

False. Let k be the indicator of the positive integers. It is measurable, bounded by one and zero almost everywhere, so its Lebesgue integral on (0,∞) is zero. E (Topology)

Words: 593 Articles: 4
2011 OurBigBook.com

E3

Words: 364 Articles: 1
E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 364
E3 OurBigBook.com
A connected space has no separation into two disjoint nonempty open subsets whose union is the space. A continuous surjection to the discrete space {0,1} produces such a separation by the two point preimages. Conversely, from a separation define a function equal to zero on one open piece and one on the other; it is continuous and surjective. Thus these formulations of connectedness are equivalent.
An interval in R is connected: if a continuous map from it to {0,1} took both values, the intermediate value theorem would force value 1/2, impossible. Conversely, a subset of R that is not an interval has points a<b in it and a point c∈(a,b) outside it. Intersecting it with (−∞,c) and (c,∞) separates it. The empty set is connected, and singleton intervals are included.
For the union assertion, any separation of X must put each nonempty connected Ai​ entirely on one side, since intersecting the separation with Ai​ would otherwise disconnect it. Pairwise nonempty intersections force all the Ai​ onto the same side. Their union is X, contradicting a nonempty second side. The empty-union case is already connected.
The plane is the union of all lines through the origin. Each line is homeomorphic to R and connected, and every pair meets at the origin, so R2 is connected. For the punctured plane, let R+​ be the positive horizontal ray, and for each r>0 let Cr​ be the circle of radius r. Each circle is a continuous image of [0,2π] and hence connected; Cr​∪R+​ is connected because its two connected pieces meet at (r,0). These unions all contain R+​ and cover the punctured plane, proving it connected as well.
Finally suppose a continuous injection g:R2→R existed. Its image is a connected interval, since a continuous image of a connected space is connected. It contains at least three distinct values; choose p whose value lies strictly between two others. The punctured plane R2∖{p} is connected by translation of the preceding result. By injectivity its image is precisely g(R2)∖{g(p)}, which is disconnected by the missing interior point. This contradicts connectedness of a continuous image. Therefore
There is no continuous injection R2→R.​
(37)

E4

Words: 229 Articles: 1
E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 229
E4 OurBigBook.com
A sequentially compact space is one in which every sequence has a subsequence converging to a point of the space. A limit point ℓ of S means every open ball around ℓ meets S∖{ℓ}.
In a compact metric space, a sequence with a finite set of values has a constant subsequence. If its value set is infinite and had no limit point, each point of the space would have a neighbourhood containing at most one point of that value set. A finite subcover would then make the value set finite, a contradiction. It therefore has a limit point in the space, and the permitted subsequence result gives a convergent subsequence. This proves sequential compactness.
For the remaining assertions assume the compact space is nonempty, as required for a fixed-point claim. The displacement function q(x)=d(f(x),x) is continuous by the stated continuity of the metric and of f. The extreme value theorem gives a minimum δ=q(p). If δ>0, then p=f(p), and strict decrease of distances implies
q(f(p))=d(f2(p),f(p))<d(f(p),p)=δ,
(38)
contradicting minimality. Thus δ=0 and p is a fixed point. Two distinct fixed points would satisfy d(p,q)=d(f(p),f(q))<d(p,q), also impossible. Hence the fixed point is unique.
On the noncompact real line, take
f(x)=log(1+ex).​
(39)

For z∈/S, neither root has modulus a, and their product is a2, so exactly one root has modulus greater than a. Selecting that root defines the exterior inverse.
More explicitly, define s(z)=z2−4a2​ to be the branch analytic on C∖S normalized by s(z)/z→1 at infinity. It is positive for real z>2a and negative for real z<−2a. Then
g(z)=2z+s(z)​.​

Existence and analyticity of this branch also follow from the exterior inverse: J′(ζ)=1−a2/ζ2 is nonzero for ∣ζ∣>a, so the selected simple root varies analytically; s=2g−z has the stated normalization. The exterior map is injective because J(ζ1​)=J(ζ2​) with distinct roots would imply ζ1​ζ2​=a2, impossible for two exterior points. Thus g is a conformal bijection throughout C∖S.
The proposed potential is a uniform stream plus its cylinder doublet and the circulation term. On ζ=aeiθ, the first two terms sum to the real quantity 2Uacos(θ−α), while the imaginary part of the logarithmic term is the constant −Γloga/(2π). Thus the cylinder is a streamline. At infinity the complex velocity tends to Ue−iα and the circulation is Γ, verifying both far-field conditions. Logarithms may be chosen locally; their derivative gives a single-valued velocity.
Composition therefore gives the plate potential
w(z)=U(g(z)e−iα+g(z)a2eiα​)−2πiΓ​logg(z).​

At the edge z=2a, corresponding to ζ=a, the physical complex velocity is W′(ζ)/J′(ζ). Since the denominator has a simple zero, finiteness requires

which is exactly

u−iv=Ucosα,or (u,v)=(Ucosα,0).​

A characteristic function is useful for proving convergence in distribution, including for laws without a finite moment-generating function: the continuity theorem says that pointwise convergence of characteristic functions to a characteristic function continuous at zero implies convergence in distribution to its law. For example, the Cauchy distribution has a characteristic function although its moment-generating function is not finite on any neighbourhood of zero.
A moment-generating function is especially useful for exponential tail bounds: for t>0 where it is finite, Markov's inequality gives
Pr(X≥a)≤e−taMX​(t).​

Optimizing over t yields a Chernoff bound. The positive real exponential in this argument permits the inequality; a unit-modulus complex exponential does not give the corresponding tail bound.

Given Xn​=k, the next child takes a fresh uniform choice from 1,…,k, making Xn+1​ uniform on 0,…,k−1. At zero the count stays zero. This conditional law depends only on the current count, so Xn​ is a Markov chain.
The amounts taken do not generally retain that state information. For N≥3, compare two positive-probability histories with the same current value Y2​=1: if Y1​=N−2, exactly one sticker remains and Y3​=1; if Y1​=N−1, none remains and Y3​=0. Thus the next amount depends on earlier history even after conditioning on the current amount, violating the Markov property.
The non-Markov assertion needs this nondegenerate range of N. With N=1 the amount process is trivial; for N=2 it is also Markov if time-inhomogeneous transitions are permitted. The history counterexample establishes the intended failure for every N≥3.

Suppose a graph satisfying Ore's theorem were not Hamiltonian. Extend it, on the same vertices, to an edge-maximal non-Hamiltonian graph H. Adding edges preserves the degree-sum hypothesis. The complete graph is Hamiltonian, so H has a missing edge uv. By maximality, H+uv has a Hamiltonian cycle, which must use the new edge. Removing it gives a Hamiltonian path in H, labelled u=v1​,v2​,…,vn​=v.
If some i has both edges uvi+1​ and vvi​, the path can be closed into the cycle
v1​,v2​,…,vi​,vn​,vn−1​,…,vi+1​,v1​,
(119)
contradicting the choice of H. Thus the index sets {i:uvi+1​∈E(H)} and {i:vvi​∈E(H)} are disjoint subsets of {1,…,n−1}. Their sizes are degH​u and degH​v. Consequently degH​u+degH​v≤n−1, contradicting the degree-sum condition for the nonadjacent pair u,v. Hence the original graph is Hamiltonian.

Represent the two sides of the marriage problem as the parts L,R of a bipartite graph, with an edge for each allowed pairing. A matching is a set of edges with no common endpoint; a complete matching of L covers every vertex in L. When the two parts have equal size it also covers R, giving a perfect matching.
Hall's marriage theorem gives the exact finite-graph criterion:
∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣for every S⊆L.​

The assertion is false for the algorithm as printed. Its second output depends only on V. For 0<V≤1/2 its sine factor is nonnegative. For 1/2<V<1, its radius is at most 2log2​, so in every case Y≥−2log2​. Therefore Pr(Y<−2)=0, whereas a standard normal variable has positive probability below −2. The printed output cannot be a pair of independent standard normals.
The minimal correction is to use U in both logarithms. Let R=−2logU​, Θ=2πV, and set X=RcosΘ, Y=RsinΘ. Independence of U,V gives independent R,Θ with densities re−r2/2 for r>0 and 1/(2π) for the angle. The polar-coordinate Jacobian is r, so the joint Cartesian density is

a OurBigBook.com
Compare every complete row with the given vector, returning as soon as a match is found. The length check prevents recycling of the vector; seq_len also handles an empty matrix correctly. This implementation treats a missing comparison as a nonmatch and always returns a Boolean.
row.match <- function(X, y) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(X), length(y) == ncol(X))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(X))) {
    eq <- X[i, ] == y
    if (all(!is.na(eq) & eq)) return(TRUE)
  }
  FALSE
}
For the integer-coordinate matrices used below there are no missing values, so this is ordinary exact row equality.

Solution
Words: 191
i OurBigBook.com
The recursive worker extends a current path by one uniformly selected unused neighbour. A trapped extension returns NULL all the way to the outer loop, which restarts from the origin. It does not backtrack and try a different branch of the same attempt, since the stated process restarts the entire walk.
saw <- function(N) {
  stopifnot(length(N) == 1L, is.finite(N), N >= 0,
            N == floor(N))
  steps <- rbind(c(1L, 0L), c(-1L, 0L),
                 c(0L, 1L), c(0L, -1L))
  grow <- function(path) {
    if (nrow(path) == N + 1L) return(path)
    last <- path[nrow(path), ]
    candidates <- sweep(steps, 2L, last, "+")
    keep <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(candidates)), function(i) {
      !row.match(path, candidates[i, ])
    }, logical(1))
    candidates <- candidates[keep, , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(candidates) == 0L) return(NULL)
    j <- sample.int(nrow(candidates), 1L)
    grow(rbind(path, candidates[j, ]))
  }
  repeat {
    path <- grow(matrix(c(0L, 0L), nrow = 1L))
    if (!is.null(path)) return(path)
  }
}
The base case has exactly N+1 visited vertices. Every extension is a unit horizontal or vertical step to a new vertex, proving the output dimensions and self-avoidance by induction. A straight path has positive probability, so each independent attempt has a positive chance of success and repeated attempts terminate almost surely.
ii
Words: 113 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 113
ii OurBigBook.com
The scheme is not uniform in general. A particular successful path has probability equal to the product of the reciprocals of its available-neighbour counts. Those counts depend on the path geometry.
For length four, the straight path (0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(4,0) has probability 1/(4⋅3⋅3⋅3)=1/108. The path (0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1),(−1,1) has only two available neighbours at its last choice, because the previous point and the origin block two directions. Its probability is 1/(4⋅3⋅3⋅2)=1/72. There is no trapping before four steps, so these are already the output probabilities. They differ, disproving uniformity on S4​.
At lengths where restarts occur, conditioning an attempt on success normalizes these path probabilities by a common success probability; it does not remove the unequal products.
iii
Words: 130 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 130
iii OurBigBook.com
A simple square-lattice polygon has even perimeter at least four. Generate a self-avoiding walk of length M−1, reject unless its endpoint is a neighbour of the origin, then add the final edge to close it.
sap <- function(M) {
  stopifnot(length(M) == 1L, is.finite(M), M >= 4,
            M == floor(M), M %% 2 == 0)
  repeat {
    path <- saw(M - 1L)
    if (sum(abs(path[nrow(path), ])) == 1L) {
      return(rbind(path, c(0L, 0L)))
    }
  }
}
The output has M+1 coordinate rows and M unit edges. The first M vertices are distinct by the call to saw; the last row repeats only the origin. Neighbouring lattice edges cannot create an additional crossing without a repeated vertex. A rectangle of perimeter M exists for every permitted even M, giving a positive probability of eventual acceptance.
